title: Packaging & dependencies for deploy
summary: Make your GenAI app deployable: declare metadata and dependencies in pyproject.toml, pin versions for reproducible builds, isolate with a virtualenv, and containerise it for the cloud.
objectives: Describe a Python project with a pyproject.toml file
Explain why pinning dependency versions makes builds reproducible
Separate loose requirements from a fully pinned lock for deployment
Use a virtual environment to isolate a project's dependencies
Write a Dockerfile that containerises a FastAPI GenAI service
Keep secrets like API keys out of the image and pass them at runtime

quiz.q: What is the modern, standard file for declaring a Python project's metadata and dependencies?
quiz.why: pyproject.toml is the standardised project file (PEP 621) where you declare name, version, dependencies, and build configuration.

quiz.q: Why pin exact dependency versions for a deployable app?
options: It makes the app run faster
It makes builds reproducible — the same versions install today and in six months, avoiding 'works on my machine' drift
It reduces the number of dependencies
It is required by Python to import packages
quiz.why: Pinning exact versions means every build installs the identical dependency set, so a build that passes today still behaves the same later and in production.

quiz.q: Why should an API key never be baked into a Docker image?
options: Anyone who pulls the image can read the secret, and it ends up in image layers and registries
quiz.why: Secrets baked into an image are readable by anyone with the image and persist in layer history; pass them at runtime via environment variables or a secrets manager instead.

quiz.q: What does a virtual environment give a project at deploy time?
options: An isolated set of dependencies so the project's packages don't clash with anything else on the host
quiz.why: A virtualenv isolates the project's installed packages so versions never collide with the system Python or other projects.

quiz.q: In one sentence, why use a pinned lock file in addition to your pyproject dependencies?
quiz.answer: pyproject lists the direct dependencies you want, while a lock file records the exact resolved versions of every package including transitive ones, so deployments are byte-for-byte reproducible.
quiz.why: Direct requirements can resolve to different transitive versions over time; a lock freezes the entire resolved tree for reproducible installs.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of copying and installing dependencies before copying your app code in a Dockerfile?
quiz.answer: It lets Docker cache the dependency layer, so rebuilds after a code change skip reinstalling unchanged dependencies and are much faster.
quiz.why: Docker caches layers in order; putting rarely-changing dependency installs first means code edits don't bust the dependency cache.

body_markdown:
## From 'runs on my laptop' to 'runs in the cloud'

You've built an async, typed FastAPI service that calls Claude. The last gap is the one every engineer knows: making it run *reliably somewhere other than your laptop*. That means declaring what your project is and what it needs, freezing those needs so they don't drift, and wrapping it in a container the cloud can run. None of this is GenAI-specific — it's the production discipline that turns a prototype into a deployable artifact.

## Describe the project: pyproject.toml

The standard project file is **`pyproject.toml`**. It declares your app's name, version, and dependencies in one place.

```toml
[project]
name = "summariser-api"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.11"
dependencies = [
    "fastapi>=0.115",
    "uvicorn>=0.30",
    "anthropic>=0.40",
    "pydantic>=2.7",
]
```

This replaces the older scattered `setup.py`/`setup.cfg`. Modern tools like **uv** or **pip** read it directly. `dependencies` lists what you *want*; the exact versions get resolved at install time.

## Pin for reproducible builds

Loose ranges like `>=0.115` are fine for development, but a deployment must be **reproducible**: the same versions today, in six months, and in production. So you also produce a **lock** — a fully pinned list of every package, including the transitive ones you never named.

```bash
# with uv
uv lock
uv export --no-dev > requirements.txt   # fully pinned

# or with pip-tools / pip freeze
pip freeze > requirements.txt
```

Now `requirements.txt` pins `fastapi==0.115.6`, `anthropic==0.42.0`, and everything underneath. This kills 'works on my machine': the build that passes CI installs the *exact* same tree in production.

## Isolate with a virtual environment

Every build still runs inside a **virtual environment** so the project's packages never clash with the host or another project.

```bash
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate   # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

The container does the same thing in a clean base image — isolation by construction.

## Containerise it

A **Dockerfile** is the recipe to build a runnable image. Order matters: install dependencies *before* copying your code so Docker can cache that layer and rebuilds stay fast.

```dockerfile
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app

# 1. Deps first — cached unless requirements change
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# 2. Then the app code
COPY . .

EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["uvicorn", "main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]
```

Build and run it:

```bash
docker build -t summariser-api .
docker run -p 8000:8000 -e ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=$ANTHROPIC_API_KEY summariser-api
```

## Never bake in secrets

Notice the API key is passed at **runtime** with `-e`, not written into the image. A secret baked into an image is readable by anyone who pulls it and lingers in layer history and registries. In the cloud you'd inject it from a secrets manager — AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault — exactly as you already do for other services. The SDK reads `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` from the environment automatically.

## Your task

Write a `pyproject.toml` for your summariser service, produce a fully pinned `requirements.txt`, and write a Dockerfile that installs dependencies before copying code. Build the image, run it passing `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` at runtime, and confirm the `/docs` page loads from the container.

slides.title: Describe it: pyproject.toml
bullets: The standard project file (PEP 621).
Name, version, Python version, dependencies.
Replaces scattered setup.py / setup.cfg.
Read by modern tools like uv and pip.
slides.narration: The standard way to describe a Python project is a single file, pyproject dot toml. In it you declare your app's name, its version, the Python version it needs, and its dependencies, all in one place. This replaces the older, scattered setup dot p y and setup dot c f g files you may have seen. Modern tools like uv and pip read it directly. The dependencies list here says what you want; the exact versions get resolved when you install.

slides.title: Direct vs transitive dependencies
bullets: You name fastapi; it pulls in dozens more.
Those unnamed ones are transitive dependencies.
pyproject lists what you chose directly.
A lock file freezes the entire resolved tree.
slides.narration: Before we pin anything, one idea you must hold onto. When you list fastapi as a dependency, you don't just install fastapi. It quietly pulls in dozens of other packages it relies on, and those pull in more. The ones you named yourself are your direct dependencies; everything underneath is transitive. Your pyproject file only lists the direct ones, the choices you made. But a deployment depends on the whole tree, and any of those transitive packages could change version on you. That's the gap a lock file closes.

slides.title: Pin for reproducible builds
bullets: Loose ranges are fine for development.
Deployment must be reproducible.
Lock every package, including transitive ones.
Kills 'works on my machine'.
slides.code:
uv lock
uv export --no-dev > requirements.txt
# or:
pip freeze > requirements.txt
slides.narration: Loose version ranges like greater-or-equal zero point one one five are fine while you develop. But a deployment must be reproducible: the exact same versions today, in six months, and in production. So alongside your pyproject you produce a lock, a fully pinned list of every single package, including the transitive ones you never named yourself. Now your requirements file pins fastapi to one precise version, anthropic to another, everything nailed down. This is what kills the dreaded works on my machine, because C I and production install the identical tree.

slides.title: Isolate with a virtualenv
bullets: A clean, isolated set of packages.
No clash with the host or other projects.
Install your pinned requirements into it.
The container does this by construction.
slides.code:
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
slides.narration: Every build still runs inside a virtual environment, the same habit you formed back in Module One, so the project's packages never clash with the host machine or another project. You create it, activate it, and install your pinned requirements into it. The lovely thing is a container does exactly this for you by construction: it starts from a clean base image, so the isolation is built in. The virtualenv idea and the container idea are really the same idea at two scales.

slides.title: Containerise it
bullets: A Dockerfile is the recipe for an image.
Install deps BEFORE copying code.
That lets Docker cache the deps layer.
CMD runs uvicorn on 0.0.0.0.
slides.code:
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["uvicorn", "main:app",
     "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]
slides.narration: A Dockerfile is the recipe to build a runnable image. Notice the order, because it matters. We copy the requirements file and install dependencies first, before copying our application code. Why? Docker caches each layer in order. Dependencies change rarely, but your code changes constantly. By installing deps first, a quick code edit doesn't force a slow reinstall of everything. Then the final command runs uvicorn, binding to zero dot zero dot zero dot zero so it's reachable from outside the container.

slides.title: Never bake in secrets
bullets: Pass ANTHROPIC_API_KEY at runtime with -e.
A baked-in secret is readable by anyone.
It lingers in layers and registries.
Inject from Secrets Manager / Key Vault.
slides.code:
docker build -t summariser-api .
docker run -p 8000:8000 \
  -e ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=$ANTHROPIC_API_KEY \
  summariser-api
slides.narration: One rule you must never break: secrets do not go in the image. See how we pass the Anthropic A P I key at runtime with dash e, an environment variable, rather than writing it into the Dockerfile. A secret baked into an image is readable by anyone who pulls that image, and it lingers forever in the layer history and your registry. In the cloud you'd inject it from A W S Secrets Manager or Azure Key Vault, exactly as you already do for your other services. The S D K reads that environment variable automatically.

slides.narration: Let's recap, and recap the whole module. You describe your project in pyproject dot toml, pin a lock so builds are reproducible, isolate dependencies with a virtualenv or a container, install dependencies before code so caching stays fast, and pass secrets at runtime, never baked in. Your final task: write a pyproject and a fully pinned requirements file for your summariser service, write a Dockerfile that installs deps before copying code, then build the image and run it, passing your A P I key at runtime, and confirm the docs page loads from inside the container. With that, you can take async GenAI code, expose it as a validated A P I, and ship it to the cloud. That's a real Applied GenAI Engineer skill set. Well done.
